name: TranslateWP
author: Verdi Heinz

sections.description:
TranslateWP helps you make your WordPress site available in more languages. Connect your site, choose your translation languages and add a language switcher. AI translates your page content using your site’s context and writing preferences.

Prepare translations ahead of visits or translate content when it is requested. Finished translations are reused, and changes to your source content are picked up for translation again. Your original pages stay in place: no duplicate pages, no translation tables.

Need to edit translations or use your own AI provider? Orbital (Pro) adds the translation editor, advanced SEO tools, the Side tab switcher and your own AI providers through the separate TranslateWP Pro addon.

Built by the team behind Code Snippets.

Included in the free plugin

  • AI translation with site context. Read your site during setup and guide translations with your writing preferences.
  • Your own Lexicon. Set preferred translations for product names, specialist terms and recurring phrases in each language.
  • Tone and style controls. Adjust tone, formality and creativity to suit your content.
  • Six switcher placements. Use a floating switcher, menu item, classic widget, the [twp-languages] shortcode, the Language Switcher block or a Button block configured as a switcher.
  • A translation dashboard. See indexed pages, translation progress, language coverage and work that needs attention.
  • Updates that follow your content. Source changes are picked up so translations can be refreshed.
  • Language addresses and hreflang. Give translated versions their own language addresses and identify them for search engines.
  • Roles and multisite. Choose who may edit translations, retranslate, manage settings or manage the Lexicon. Editing translated text requires the Pro translation editor. Network administrators can set defaults for sites in a network.

TranslateWP requires a connected TranslateWP account and its online translation service, including on the free plan. Setup guides you through connecting your site. You do not need to change DNS or move your site.

TranslateWP Pro

Orbital (Pro) extends the free plugin with the separate TranslateWP Pro addon:

  • Translation editor. Review and correct translated text on your site.
  • Advanced SEO tools. Manage translated metadata and slugs, image alt text and additional search-engine options.
  • Side tab switcher. Offer a language tab along the edge of the page.
  • Additional writing controls. Refine translations for your audience, length and cultural adaptation.
  • Your own AI providers. Connect supported providers and choose a fallback order for each language. Your provider bills for that usage.

The addon requires an eligible TranslateWP account. Once eligibility is confirmed, the free plugin offers to install it. Installing the addon by itself does not unlock Pro features.

Plans and fair use

Every plan includes AI translation with a fair-use allowance per 30 days. When your account reaches its allowance, translated pages keep working for visitors and new translation pauses until the window moves on. On Orbital, add your own AI key to keep going.

  • Terrestrial (Free): Fair-use allowance per 30 days.
  • Orbital (Pro): A higher fair-use allowance. Add your own AI key for more volume, billed by your provider.
  • Universal (Agency): Agreed with you, above the Orbital allowance.

Visit TranslateWP for plan information.

Support and contributions

  • WordPress.org support forum
  • Source code and bug reports
  • Translate the plugin interface

Find TranslateWP useful? Leave a review on WordPress.org to help others decide whether it suits their site.

External services and privacy

TranslateWP connects to api.translatewp.ai to register your connected site, generate and retrieve translations, report translation progress and check which features your account may use.

The plugin also uses app.translatewp.ai, the TranslateWP account portal, to sign in and connect your site, view account information and access plans and upgrades.

After account eligibility is confirmed, the free plugin can download, install and update the Pro addon package from the TranslateWP service.

Translation and site-reading features send the page content selected for processing, along with information such as the site host, home URL, selected languages and translation instructions. The service processes that content to provide translations. This includes content supplied in the site’s context and Lexicon when it is needed for a translation.

The plugin also sends sampled translation timing, completion and count measurements to help diagnose delivery performance. These performance reports do not contain page text or full page URLs.

When you connect your site or use these features, the TranslateWP service is involved. Review what you make available for translation and exclude private or sensitive content that should not be processed before scanning or translating your site.

Using your own AI provider on Pro also makes the provider’s terms and privacy policy relevant to the content it processes.

  • TranslateWP service terms
  • TranslateWP privacy policy
sections.installation:
Automatic Installation

  1. Open Plugins > Add New and search for TranslateWP.
  2. Click Install Now, then Activate.
  3. Open TranslateWP in the admin menu and follow setup to connect your account, read your site, choose your writing preferences and select your languages.
  4. Configure your language switcher and check a translated page.

Manual Installation

  1. Download the plugin ZIP and upload it through Plugins > Add New > Upload Plugin, or unzip it and upload the translate directory to wp-content/plugins/.
  2. Activate TranslateWP and complete setup from its admin menu.

Multisite Installation

Network activate TranslateWP from Network Admin to use the network settings and defaults. Check each site’s connection, languages and settings before offering translations to visitors.
sections.faq:
Do I need a TranslateWP account?

Yes. The plugin connects to the TranslateWP service to generate and serve translations. The setup wizard guides you through connecting your account and site. A paid plan is not required to use the free features.

Does it translate every page into every language at once?

TranslateWP can prepare translations in the background and request translations when content is needed. You can follow progress in the Dashboard. A page that is still being translated may take longer than one whose translation is already ready.

What happens when I edit my original content?

TranslateWP detects source changes and queues updated content for translation. Check the Dashboard for progress; a source edit does not mean every language is ready immediately.

Can I control product names and specialist terms?

Yes. Add them to your Lexicon and set the wording you want in each language. You can also adjust the writing settings. The Pro translation editor lets you correct translated text directly.

Does it work with my theme or page builder?

TranslateWP works with rendered page text rather than requiring a separate translated copy of each post. Test your theme, builder and interactive elements on a staging site. Compatibility can depend on how a theme or plugin renders and updates its content.

Can search engines find translated pages?

Translated versions have language addresses and hreflang links. Search visibility also depends on your site’s indexing settings and translation readiness. Pro adds advanced SEO controls, including translated metadata and slugs. No plugin can guarantee indexing or rankings.

Will my page cache need configuration?

Your cache must keep different language addresses separate. If your site still uses ?lang= addresses, do not strip the language parameter or serve the default-language page for it. Check translated pages with your cache enabled, especially after changing cache rules.

Are translations stored as duplicate WordPress pages?

No. TranslateWP adds no translation tables and no duplicate pages. Your original posts and pages remain the content you edit.

Can I use my own AI provider?

Yes, with Orbital (Pro) and the Pro addon. Connect a supported provider in the AI models settings and choose the providers for each language. Your provider’s own charges and terms apply.

Does installing the Pro addon activate a paid plan?

No. Pro features require an eligible TranslateWP account as well as the addon. The free plugin offers installation after checking eligibility.

Where can I get help?

Use the plugin’s Support screen or the WordPress.org support forum. Report reproducible bugs on GitHub.
sections.changelog:
0.10.30

  • Who can manage translations: in Translations > Settings, give each role any of four rights: edit translations, retranslate, manage the settings and manage the Lexicon. Administrators hold all four. On a network, set defaults for every site, let a site change them, or lock them. “Also these users” gives chosen users the settings and the Lexicon, and “Who sees translations” is gone: every visitor sees translations.
  • Edit mode shows each user the rows their rights allow, and a new “Retranslate this page” row sends the page you are on again in every language, after asking once more.
  • The site name menu in the toolbar links to TranslateWP, on the site and in wp-admin, for anyone with a TranslateWP screen: an administrator reaches the Dashboard, others their Settings or the Lexicon. On a network, My Sites links each site to the screen you have there.
  • Pro: while Side tab is the chosen switcher type, edit mode no longer offers Switcher placement; drag the tab along the screen edges instead.
  • Translations > Settings: Content and Behaviour sit side by side on a wide screen, and Audience carries a sparkle while Pro is active.

0.10.29

  • A file a visitor’s browser fetches (a script, a data file, robots or llms text) is never indexed as a page.
  • Plainer words on the Dashboard, the Indexing page and the Lexicon: the day’s figure says what it counts, pages waiting for your latest change are named as such, a language’s progress reads “28 of 28 translated”, and a suggested term that no translation has used yet says so in one line.
  • The site’s own language is never translated into, and pages of a language removed from the list are left alone: they no longer show on the Indexing page, and Retry does not send them again.
  • The Dashboard counts a page translation as done when its translation finished and keeps that count: it no longer drops to zero and climbs again after time away, a change to the brief or the lexicon is retranslated only when you say so, and pages that could not be delivered are listed with a Retry.
  • The reposition badge is part of the switcher’s grab area. The switcher’s small “by TranslateWP” line has a Support TranslateWP switch, in edit mode and in Languages > Switcher: off by default on Pro, always on with Terrestrial.
  • Pro: a third switcher type, Side tab. The switcher is a tab on the edge of the screen and the languages slide out from it; in edit mode you drag it along the edges, separately for wide screens and phones. Switchers placed in the page stay dropdowns.
  • A customer’s order email keeps the address exactly as entered: the state and country codes are values, never words to translate.
  • An account that already includes Pro sees Install Pro or Activate Pro beside a locked feature, in setup and in the settings, never the Pro tag; the setup wizard knows it from the first moment, so its prompt never asks to buy again. After installing from a locked preset, the setup comes back with that preset chosen.

  • Pro: a switch in Settings > AI models lets the TranslateWP model translate while the plan’s quota lasts and your own providers take over once it is exhausted; a translation job that switched stays with them until it ends, and new jobs return to the TranslateWP model when the quota resets.

  • The plugins screen says to delete TranslateWP Pro first while Pro is installed, instead of offering to delete TranslateWP, on a single site and on the network.

  • The language pickers no longer offer plain English; choose the English of a region. A site that already uses plain English keeps it.
  • The switcher’s dropdown widens to fit long language names, within the room its place on the screen leaves.
  • Settings > Translation: the style sliders have a real handle you can drag or move with the keyboard, and choosing a tone moves Formality to that tone’s level (Casual, Friendly, Professional, Formal). You can still move it afterwards.
  • Setup compares the work with a human translator at 2.5 hours per page per language, in working weeks, days and hours.
  • The Dashboard links to the pages still waiting while a translation runs, and the Indexing list says since when a page has been translating, or that it is waiting its turn.
  • Support: the ticket shows the reply address and lets you change it. The plan chip opens your account, the help cards sit side by side, the advice about other translation plugins is a notice, and clearing the cache says what happens next.
  • Switcher settings: the preview sits beside the options, the option cards no longer jump, and the native dropdown no longer breaks when flags are turned on.
  • Pro: the Side tab’s drag handle sits in the middle of the tab, and the tab follows the pointer smoothly.

0.10.28

  • Answer engines may index translations from the start: the preset is on for a site that never chose, and robots.txt opens every translated language to them. A site that turned it off keeps its choice.
  • A translation the service has not served within a minute is left for a later visit: the page stops asking every two seconds and no element stays marked as loading.
  • The Pro editor anchors the switcher to any element, above, below, left or right of it; the switcher then follows that element, in a footer or a sticky header alike. A new switcher setting chooses what a page without the anchored element shows, and the Dashboard names such pages.

0.10.27

  • The browser’s Back and Forward buttons move between the language addresses a visitor switched through, and the page follows the address it lands on.
  • A page served with a translated title tells the runtime its source title, so a language switch translates the title from the source and the tab title follows the switch.
  • Text a widget copies from an already translated element is served from the cache under the original’s own key, and nodes that appear while a translation is in flight are served together in one round trip.
  • The 404 page’s translated title is served on every missing address, not only on the page the index read.
  • A crawler’s translated page keeps image alt text as written on a site without Pro, as the visitor’s page does.
  • The languages step of setup states how many page translations the chosen languages commit to and how much of the quota is available, before anything is translated.
  • A correction saved in the Pro editor is stored under the cache’s own marker ids, so it is served on every later visit.
  • A browser whose local translation store cannot be opened translates the page without it instead of waiting forever.
  • A switcher placed anywhere on the page with the Pro editor is found again on a visitor’s page, which has no admin bar.
  • Retranslating with the current Lexicon terms states the page translations it counts and the quota available, like the other retranslation prompts.

0.10.26

  • The switcher stays where it is dropped; the drag handle shows a move icon.

0.10.25

  • The last setup step shows a progress bar with the time taken and what a translator would need for the same work; every language has its own flag button that fills as its pages translate.
  • The site language sits on the connection line of the setup, proposed by the read of your site and editable on every step; a new read replaces the brief instead of adding to it.
  • The 404 page is read and translated like every other page, for visitors and crawlers alike.
  • The message shown while a page is still translating can be edited in the switcher settings.
  • Comments, menus and widgets can be left untranslated, per site or across a network.
  • Pro: translations can be shown only to chosen roles, per site or across a network; audience, length and cultural adaptation join the style settings; the setup offers the Pro presets.
  • Latin American Spanish joins the language list, and every regional variety is translated in its own spelling and vocabulary.
  • Translating again asks with the quota it uses and a plain go-ahead; the Support report leads with the plugin events.
  • The plugin keeps its scripts out of the delay and defer settings of WP Rocket, LiteSpeed Cache and Perfmatters, so the switcher shows before the first click, and another plugin’s styles no longer blank its own.
  • Text a theme copies from a translation is no longer sent as new source text.

0.10.24

  • The setup wizard’s connect step shows the three steps as a numbered path, in the same style as the account portal.

0.10.23

  • The setup wizard’s connect step explains the three steps ahead; the last step finishes from its own card and links to the translated homepage in up to three languages.
  • The translation step reports how many pages were translated into how many languages, and in how long.
  • A Support tab replaces Activity: the feedback form, a support report to copy or paste, and support tickets by email on Pro.
  • The Dashboard’s Today cards explain cached segments and the cache ratio; the Lexicon card offers the first term when empty.
  • Settings pages share one layout of cards: the switcher preview pins while the settings scroll, flag styles show samples, and the colours follow the account portal.
  • Legal, Medical, Playful and Luxury presets are Pro; the native select switcher carries emoji flags and its own chevron.
  • The network settings page uses the site admin layout, shows the network at a glance, lists sites with their setup state, and lets Pro apply the main site switcher position to every subsite.
  • My Sites in the admin bar opens each site’s TranslateWP dashboard and the network settings.
  • Titles and site names with special characters read correctly everywhere.
  • The plugin package no longer ships vendor housekeeping files.

0.10.22

  • Translated pages live at language folder addresses such as /de/; the old lang parameter redirects there, and hreflang and canonical tags use the folder address.
  • All six switcher placements are free: the floating widget, the nav-menu item, the block, the button toggle, the shortcode and the classic widget.
  • Setup has five steps: Connect, Read your site, Style and tone, Languages and Translation. Reading stops at 25 pages, and the homepage is translated first and shown beside the status in a language you choose.
  • A site admin can let users who edit pages manage translations, the Lexicon and the switcher.
  • WooCommerce order emails are sent in the language the customer shopped in.
  • Every plan can export the site’s translations from Settings.
  • Password-protected and private pages are not translated by default, and any page can be excluded in its editor.
  • A crawler on a translated address gets the complete translation, or the original page with a canonical tag and a retry hint.
  • The Dashboard shows the account’s translation quota as a percentage.
  • Image alt text translation moves to Pro; a site that used it on the free plan is told once. The Pro SEO options show as locked rows.
  • Deleting the plugin from a connected site disconnects it on the service. Deactivating or deleting the plugin removes every scheduled task, and with “Delete data on uninstall” on, every option and transient; on a network, only the network setting decides.
  • A cold page reports its title with the rest, and nothing looks the cache up again after the stream.
  • The readme carries the fair-use wording.
  • Migrations run on init, so an update no longer fails on sites whose menus are read during the update.

Earlier releases are listed in changelog.txt in the plugin folder.
